title: OpenAI just published 722 math papers written by an AI
ticker: Google halves Nano Banana image prices
Sierra and Meta publish Personal Agent Protocol

scenes.narration: Did you know that OpenAI just published seven hundred twenty-two math papers? And an AI wrote every single one.

On October seventh, OpenAI posted them on GitHub, free for anyone to read. They're grouped into three hundred seventy-two families, and came from an unreleased model that was handed about four thousand problems.
scenes.headline: OpenAI publishes 722 AI-written math manuscripts, free on GitHub

scenes.narration: And on average, each paper took about three hours of AI thinking. That's one afternoon of compute per result.
scenes.label: AI thinking per paper
scenes.sub: Average per result, from an unreleased OpenAI model.

scenes.narration: So how do you trust a paper no human wrote? That's where Lean comes in. Lean is a proof checker: software that verifies every logical step of a proof.
scenes.definition: Software that checks every logical step of a math proof.

scenes.narration: Some of these papers come with Lean proofs, so a computer has checked them. Others don't yet, and the repository itself warns they could contain mistakes.

left.title: Lean-checked
points: Trust the proof, not the author

right.title: Not formalized yet
points: README says it may have issues

scenes.verdict: Some are proven. Others still need checking.

scenes.narration: Quick pause. If this is blowing your mind, hit like, and share it with a friend who thinks AI can't do math.
scenes.line: Hit like. Share with a math-loving friend.
scenes.sub: A new AI story every morning.

scenes.narration: OpenAI's own readme is blunt: Not all have accompanying Lean formalizations. Some of the unformalized results could have issues.
scenes.text: Not all have accompanying Lean formalizations. Some of the unformalized results could have issues.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Math is a test of real reasoning. If AI can write proofs, checking them becomes the hard part. And an advisory group at the Institute for Advanced Study is urging labs to disclose their models, prompts, and costs.
points: Checking may now be harder than writing
Experts want open, shared rules for releases

scenes.narration: Three takeaways. One: seven hundred twenty-two AI-written math papers are now public. Two: some are machine-checked, some are not. Three: when AI writes it, humans still need to verify it.
points: Some are machine-checked, some are not
